investigations.name: colonies-01-hpc-readiness
investigations.description:
Build phase fixed daughter-process hydration so structural _add
instantiates daughter EcoliWCMs through the engine. Decide phase
N-sweep (N ∈ {1,2,4,8}) on one machine measured per-tick wall,
per-cell cost, peak RSS, and pymunk step — extrapolated to a
cells-per-HPC-node budget and identified the GIL as the dominant
bottleneck. Output: 384 cells/node sweet spot on 64-core/256GB.

investigations.name: pdmp-00-characterization
investigations.description:
Phase 0 of the v2ecoli → PDMP roadmap. The deliverables of this
study become the validation standard for every subsequent phase:
a replacement subprocess (Phase 1 ODE metabolism, Phase 2 jump
transcription, etc.) is accepted when its interface statistics
match the Phase 0 reference Xarray dataset within tolerance.

No biological mechanism is changed in this study — v2ecoli is run
as-is. The artefacts produced are (a) the typed interface schema
library, (b) the reference Xarray datasets across the ≥3 chosen
conditions, and (c) the per-step profiling report.

Conditions are not yet locked; tentative set: aerobic M9 + glucose
(the canonical reference), aerobic M9 + acetate (slower growth,
gluconeogenic flux), aerobic M9 + glucose + amino-acid mix (faster
growth, partial relief on translation). The DUF report Sec. 4.1.1
notes "approximately a dozen environmental conditions" exist in
the current WCM; we sample three that span the metabolic regime.

# Numerical considerations
The reference Xarray datasets are not single trajectories — they
are *ensembles*. For each (condition, seed) pair we run N=64
independent stochastic replicates (justification: the standard
error of an estimated mean falls as σ/√N ≈ σ/8 = 12.5% of σ, fine
enough to set a Wasserstein-2 tolerance band that downstream
phases can target without overfitting to MC noise). Replicate
count revisited after running pilot N=8 batches and measuring
per-observable variance — N is increased per-observable if MCSE
exceeds 10% of the inter-condition effect size.

Per-step compute profiling reports mean ± std over ≥1000 step
samples per condition (not single measurements), with separate
buckets for: (i) FBA LP solve time (`wholecell.utils.modular_fba`, glpk-linear), (ii) stochastic-draw RNG
cost, (iii) store↔process marshalling, (iv) topology traversal,
(v) emitter I/O. A bootstrap 95% CI on each bucket isolates
signal from machine jitter.

Variable categorization is recorded with a *numerical-sensitivity
tier* per variable: ODE-amenable variables carry an estimated
contribution to the Jacobian spectral radius (rough stiffness
signal); stochastic-discrete variables carry an empirical
per-step coefficient of variation; coupling-artifact variables
carry a coupling-strength index (the L∞ norm of the partial
derivatives across the artificial boundary).

# Emitter
All runs use **XArrayEmitter** (workspace default on this branch;
wired in dashboard via PR #70). The reference dataset is a
zarr store per (condition, replicate, generation) tuple, opened
downstream via xarray.open_zarr() with explicit chunking on the
time axis so Phase 1+ phases can stream-compare distributions
without loading the whole ensemble into memory. max_generations
in workspace.yaml is set to 8 (covers the multi-generation
lineage statistics that division-time / inheritance-distribution
validation in Phase 2 will consume).

investigations.name: pdmp-01-metabolism-ode
investigations.description:
Phase 1 of the v2ecoli → PDMP roadmap.

## What v2ecoli's metabolism actually is

v2ecoli's metabolism lives at `v2ecoli/processes/metabolism.py`
(class `Metabolism`, wrapping `FluxBalanceAnalysisModel` →
`wholecell.utils.modular_fba.FluxBalanceAnalysis` with the
`glpk-linear` solver). Each timestep it solves a SINGLE multi-
objective FBA LP that combines:

  1. **Biomass production**: `max c^T v` where `c` is the biomass
     composition vector derived from the doubling time.
  2. **Homeostatic concentration targets**: drive metabolite
     concentrations toward `conc_dict[media + doubling_time]`
     (with optional ppGpp coupling when `include_ppgpp=True`,
     linking transcriptional regulation to metabolic capacity).
  3. **Kinetic-constraint targets** (when `USE_KINETICS=True`):
     drive enzyme-catalysed reaction flux toward Vmax×[E]
     computed from per-reaction kinetic parameters and live
     substrate concentrations — coupling translation demand
     (which sets enzyme abundance) to metabolic output.

Constraints: stoichiometric mass balance `S v = 0`, enzyme-
catalysis bounds (reactions without catalysts forced to v=0,
catalysed reactions bounded by Vmax×[E]), NGAM (non-growth-
associated maintenance) ATP demand, and exchange bounds derived
from the media. Output fluxes (mmol/g_DCW/h) are converted to
molecule count changes via
`stochasticRound(flux × dry_mass × dt / (MW × conv))`. The
process runs LAST in the timestep (deriver-style, on the
post-partition state of all other processes).

This is structurally distinct from textbook "tFBA" (Birch, Udell
& Covert 2014), which is a sequence of LPs tracking target
trajectories over time. v2ecoli solves a fresh single LP per
timestep with current bounds + the multi-objective coupling
above; it does NOT carry the temporal-target-tracking structure
Birch et al. describe.

## What blocks likelihood-based inference today

The properties of v2ecoli's metabolism that make it resistant to
Bayesian inference + causal discovery:

- **stochasticRound discretisation** at the LP→counts boundary:
  a non-smooth, RNG-dependent map applied per timestep.
- **Implicit per-timestep "jumps"** when enzyme bounds change
  (because enzyme abundances change every step via gene
  expression), so consecutive LP solutions jump between vertices
  of different polytopes — discontinuous in the FBA state.
- **LP-vertex degeneracy**: GLPK returns an arbitrary vertex of
  the optimum facet, so the chosen flux distribution at the LP
  solution is degenerate. Re-runs with the same state can yield
  different flux vectors when the optimum is non-unique.
- **Doubling-time as both input AND output** without a
  separated dynamical equation — the homeostatic targets are
  parameterised by doubling-time, but doubling-time IS
  determined by the biomass-production rate the FBA computes.
- **Timestep-dependent kinetic-constraint refresh** — the
  kinetic-constraint terms re-read enzyme abundances each step,
  so the LP itself is non-autonomous in a way that's tied to
  the discrete-time loop.

The substitution target is Millard et al. 2017
([[millard2017]]) — a curated kinetic ODE of E. coli central
carbon and energy metabolism covering glycolysis (EMP),
gluconeogenesis, PPP, Entner-Doudoroff, anaplerotic reactions,
TCA, glyoxylate shunt, acetate metabolism, nucleotide
interconversion, and oxidative phosphorylation. The published
model is calibrated for K-12 MG1655 on M9 + glucose at dilution
rate 0.1 h⁻¹, pH 7.0, 37 °C, pO₂ > 20%. Calibration to other
Phase 0 conditions (acetate, glucose+aa) is part of this study.

Infrastructure: rather than re-implement the Millard 2017 rate
laws from scratch, we wrap the published SBML (BioModels
MODEL1505110000) with **pbg-copasi**
(https://github.com/vivarium-collective/pbg-copasi) — a
process-bigraph adapter that exposes any SBML kinetic model as
a `CopasiUTCProcess` (Uniform Time Course Process) or
`CopasiSteadyStateStep` via the COPASI/basico simulation
backend. This lets Phase 1 run the original Millard model as a
standalone PB process on day one, while keeping the SBML file
itself as the source of truth.

FBA-bridge composite. Because pdmp-01 cannot rip out v2ecoli's
multi-objective FBA all at once (the rest of v2ecoli expects
flux outputs in the existing store layout, and the FBA's
homeostatic + kinetic-constraint terms couple it to translation
+ transcription that we're NOT touching in Phase 1), we build a
transitional composite that couples the pbg-copasi Millard
process to v2ecoli's existing FBA. The two run side by side:
the ODE drives central-carbon flux predictions (glycolysis, PPP,
TCA, oxidative phosphorylation — the network Millard covers),
while v2ecoli's FBA handles the rest (homeostatic targets for
non-central metabolites, enzyme-catalysed reactions outside the
Millard scope, NGAM maintenance). The bridge schema is the
contract to negotiate: which fluxes does the ODE export, which
does the FBA consume, where is the seam between mechanistic-
kinetic and optimisation-based metabolism. Once the bridge holds
interface fidelity across all Phase 0 conditions, the seam can
be moved outward in subsequent studies (extend the kinetic ODE
coverage, shrink the FBA scope).

The LQR layer replaces v2ecoli's FBA biomass-production
objective with an explicit, parameterised controller around a
growth-rate target. The risk flagged in the roadmap is that the
LQR reference trajectory could reintroduce a teleonomic
parameter in disguise — parametrization of the reference
trajectory requires careful justification.

# Numerical considerations
Solver. The Millard 2017 system has stiffness from the disparity
between fast equilibration of pool intermediates (sub-second
timescales for some PPP/EMP metabolites) and slow growth-rate
dynamics (>10² s). COPASI/basico defaults to LSODA (Hindmarsh
adaptive BDF/Adams), which auto-switches between stiff and
non-stiff modes; we keep this default. Tolerances: rtol=1e-6,
atol=1e-9 (one order tighter than basico defaults) to ensure the
numerical solution error stays below the Phase 0 MC noise floor
per [[uq-bootstrap-cis-on-interface-stats]]. A Richardson
step-doubling check at fresh initial conditions confirms the
solver achieves the claimed order before any LQR tuning starts.

Distribution comparison. ODE+LQR is a deterministic process given
its initial condition; comparison with the stochastic v2ecoli
baseline goes through the Phase 0 *ensemble* of trajectories.
The acceptance criterion uses Wasserstein-2 distance W₂(p_ODE,
p_ref) per interface variable, with tolerance derived from
Phase 0 bootstrap CIs (we accept ODE output if W₂ falls within
the 95% CI of the Phase 0 self-MC W₂ spread — i.e., the ODE
must be indistinguishable from a fresh Phase 0 replicate of the
same condition).

Identifiability. Before declaring the model "inference-ready"
for Phase 3, we run a Fisher Information Matrix conditioning
check on the causal parameters (κ(FIM) < 10⁸ required) and a
profile-likelihood width estimate per parameter. Parameters that
fail are flagged non-identifiable and either re-parameterized
(lump rate constants into effective Vmax/Km pairs) or moved to
the teleonomic catalog with explicit justification.

LQR sensitivity. Sobol indices (first-order + total) on LQR
weights with respect to steady-state growth rate and key flux
ratios. A LQR weight that the system is insensitive to is "free
parameter" rot — flagged and removed.

# Emitter
All Phase 1 runs use XArrayEmitter; output zarr stores conform
to the Phase 0 reference schema (same variable names, same time-
axis convention) so xarray.align()-based comparison is
trivial. The W₂ tolerance check loads paired Phase 0 + Phase 1
zarr stores via xarray.open_zarr(..., chunks={'time': -1,
'replicate': 1}) for streaming per-replicate comparison.

investigations.name: pdmp-02-jump-processes
investigations.description:
Phase 2 of the v2ecoli → PDMP roadmap. The current discrete-time
layer is the most numerically suspect part of v2ecoli:
parametrization of stochastic draws depends on the ratio of the
fixed timestep to the teleonomic "doubling time" parameter
(DUF Sec. 4.1.1), and the global reallocation step exists to
paper over mass conservation violations introduced by the
composition of independent processes (DUF Sec. 2.1).

A PDMP-class formulation has neither: events occur at random
times drawn from explicit propensity functions, division is a
first-passage time of a continuous observable, and competition
for shared resources is encoded as state-dependent jump kernels
rather than a corrective fix-up step. The mathematical contract
to verify is that, between any two jumps, the state evolves
deterministically according to the coupled ODE (Phase 1
metabolism + any continuous components of expression machinery),
and that jumps occur at times specified by ∫ λ(s) ds = E for
E ~ Exp(1).

# Numerical considerations
Stochastic integration. Naive Gillespie SSA is exact but slow at
the propensity scales of mRNA/protein dynamics in a single cell
(10²–10⁴ events / s). The implementation choice (exact SSA vs.
τ-leaping vs. hybrid Anderson modified-next-reaction) trades
variance against compute and is justified per-process: e.g.,
ribosome-elongation events use τ-leaping with τ chosen so the
leap-condition (Δλ/λ < 0.03) holds; rare promoter-firing events
use exact next-reaction. Each choice carries a documented weak-
order and strong-order convergence claim.

Exponential-clock validation. The fundamental test of correctness
for a stochastic-jump implementation is that the cumulative
hazard ∫ λ(s) ds at successive events is Exp(1)-distributed.
We run this Anderson-Darling test over ≥10⁴ inter-event
intervals per jump process (α = 0.05). A failed test is the
smoking gun for a propensity bug.

First-passage validation. Cell division is a first-passage time
for volume crossing a threshold under the ODE+jump combined
dynamics. Before deploying on the full WCM we validate the
first-passage implementation on an analytical test problem
(Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, exact Bessel-function FPT
distribution) — the empirical FPT distribution from our
integrator must match the analytical CDF to KS distance < 0.02
over N=10⁴ trajectories.

Distribution-match resolution. Comparing trajectory ensembles
vs. v2ecoli baseline uses W₂ on summary statistic distributions
(growth rate, mean per-gene mRNA, mean per-gene protein,
division-time CV). N=200 PDMP trajectories per condition gives
W₂ MCSE ≈ σ_W₂/√200 ≈ 0.07 σ_W₂ — fine enough to detect
systematic deviations of ≥0.2 σ in the underlying distributions.
Sample size revisited if MCSE > 10% of the inter-baseline effect
size.

PDMP integrator validity. The Markov property is a structural
claim; we test it by re-simulating individual segments with the
same (state, RNG seed) and confirming bit-identical determinism
between jumps. Failure = leaky abstraction.

# Emitter
XArrayEmitter records every jump event as a row in a separate
zarr group ('jumps') alongside the continuous trajectory group
('continuous'), so the discrete-event time series and the ODE
segments can both be queried with xarray. max_generations=8 in
workspace.yaml accommodates the multi-generation division-time
CV / mother-daughter inheritance distributions that we compare
to v2ecoli baseline.

investigations.name: pdmp-03-inference
investigations.description:
Phase 3 of the v2ecoli → PDMP roadmap. With the PDMP in place
from Phase 2, every simulation trajectory is a sample from a
well-defined process measure with a constructible likelihood.
The inference-stack additions in this phase make that likelihood
observable, computable, and tractable for downstream Bayesian
workflows.

ChiRho (BasisResearch, 2024) is the reference for the algebraic-
effect interpretation of observe / intervene. The Vivarium API
analysis in the DUF report Sec. 4.2.2 noted that Vivarium can be
understood as a domain-specific algebraic effect system for
discrete-event simulation, opening a clear path to extending it
toward a PPL.

ABC-SMC is the baseline inference engine because it is robust to
highly nonlinear, partially observed dynamics — appropriate for
a first pass before more efficient gradient-based methods are
attempted in Phase 5. The structured-population layer addresses
the practical fact that omics data come from bulk cultures, not
single cells; bulk observables are expectations over the single-
cell PDMP measure.

# Numerical considerations
Likelihood library. Each modality's likelihood is parameterized
with its dispersion / overdispersion / noise scale, fit on
calibration data, and the fit reported with its 95% CI:
 - RNA-seq: NegBin(μ, φ), φ MLE'd on a held-out calibration
   dataset; expect φ ∈ [0.1, 1.0] for E. coli.
 - Proteomics: LogNormal(μ, σ²), σ from technical-replicate
   spread (typical σ_log ≈ 0.2 for SILAC/iBAQ).
 - Growth: Normal(log μ, σ_μ²) — log-scale because growth
   rates are bounded below by 0 and dispersion scales
   multiplicatively.
 - Metabolomics: Normal/LogNormal per-metabolite depending on
   dynamic range; explicit per-metabolite choice recorded.

Accumulator numerics. Log-likelihood contributions are summed
in log space throughout to avoid underflow (typical full-run
log-likelihood is ≪ -10³). Mixture-likelihood contributions
(e.g., zero-inflated NegBin) use log-sum-exp with the standard
shift trick. Pairwise / Kahan summation order for cross-cell
population reductions so the result is independent of trajectory
ordering and reproducible across hardware.

ABC-SMC schedule. ε-decay set adaptively at the quantile q=0.5
of the previous population's distance, with a minimum population
size N=1000 and a terminating ESS < 0.5·N (resample) or wall-
clock cap. Distance (PLANNED, NOT YET IMPLEMENTED — the current pilot uses an unweighted SSE/Euclidean distance with no covariance and no condition-number/kappa guard): Mahalanobis on a hand-picked summary vector
(growth rate, mean log-mRNA per high-coverage gene, mean
log-protein per high-coverage gene, key metabolite log-conc).
We report posterior ESS and the proposal acceptance rate at
every SMC step.

Posterior calibration. Simulation-Based Calibration (Talts et
al. 2018): for K=1000 SBC draws of (θ*, y*) from the prior +
forward model, run ABC-SMC and record the rank of θ* in the
posterior sample. The rank histogram must pass a χ² uniformity
test (p > 0.05) and 90% credible intervals must achieve ≥85%
empirical coverage. SBC at K=1000 has rank-resolution of 1/(K+1)
≈ 10⁻³, fine enough for typical posterior diagnostics.

Identifiability. We re-run the Phase 1 Fisher-information check
for any new parameters introduced here (likelihood dispersions,
population-layer parameters) and flag non-identifiable
combinations explicitly.

# Emitter
ABC-SMC iterates ~10⁶ PDMP runs; we use XArrayEmitter in a
"summary-only" mode that writes only the predeclared summary-
statistic vector per trajectory (zarr group 'summary'), skipping
full time-series capture. Posterior particles, per-SMC-step
ε, ESS, and proposal-acceptance trajectories also written to
zarr ('posterior'/'diagnostics' groups). SBC runs (K=1000)
produce a separate zarr store keyed by SBC iteration for
post-hoc rank-histogram analysis.

investigations.name: pdmp-04-compilation
investigations.description:
Phase 4 of the v2ecoli → PDMP roadmap. The DUF report Sec. 4.2.1
identifies that "submodel definitions and simulation modules
are currently inseparable" in v2ecoli and that the runtime
"exhibits orders of magnitude of overhead, relative to
competitive numerical solvers" — the dominant cause being
marshalling overhead from the row-centric nested-dictionary
state representation.

Catalyst.jl + ModelingToolkit + JumpProcesses.jl is the
reference target: an established Julia stack for compiled
reaction-network simulation with symbolic Jacobians and
GPU-friendly state representations. The PB → Catalyst.jl
bridge will require codifying the PB process interface as a
Catalyst-compatible reaction network spec; this is the
primary new infrastructure deliverable.

The column-centric refactor of Vivarium itself is a substantial
undertaking; the roadmap implies it can be initiated in
parallel with Phases 1–2 by an independent infrastructure team.

# Numerical considerations
Numerical equivalence. The single hardest test for a compiled
re-implementation is: does it produce the same trajectory
ensemble as the reference Phase 2 runner? "Same" means
W₂(p_compiled, p_phase2) ≤ 5·σ_MC where σ_MC is the standard
error of the Phase 2 self-W₂ estimate at the same N (a 5σ
bound is conservative — covers genuine FP-order differences
without firing on legitimate stochastic noise). We test on N=10⁴
trajectories across all Phase 0 conditions.

Precision. Single-precision (FP32) on GPU is tempting for 2×
throughput but has been shown to corrupt long-run ABC posteriors
via catastrophic cancellation in propensity sums. Default:
FP64. FP32 only allowed where (a) bit-equivalence test passes
vs FP64 reference and (b) downstream ABC posteriors are
invariant under switch.

FP summation order. Parallel reductions over per-trajectory
log-likelihoods must use a deterministic summation order
(pairwise or Kahan) so that the result is independent of GPU
thread scheduling. Non-deterministic atomic-add reductions are
banned — they break SBC reproducibility across hardware.

Convergence orders. The compiled ODE integrator and stochastic
integrator each carry an explicit convergence claim:
 - ODE: order-5 embedded Runge-Kutta (default) or BDF for
   stiff segments; verified on Van der Pol oscillator + Brusselator
   test problems before deployment.
 - SSA-based jumps: exact (no integration error).
 - τ-leaping: weak order 1, strong order 0.5; tested on
   analytical M/M/1 queue.

Throughput vs variance. The relevant performance metric for
downstream inference is not raw trajectories/second but
posterior-estimate-variance per wall-clock second. We report
both: trajectories/sec at fixed precision AND ABC posterior
variance × wall-clock-time (standard MCMC efficiency metric).
Doubling trajectories should roughly halve posterior variance
(1/√N scaling) — if not, the parallelism has hidden
correlations to investigate.

# Emitter
Compiled-runner output goes through a Julia → XArrayEmitter
bridge that batches per-trajectory results into chunked zarr
writes (chunks: {trajectory: 64, time: -1}) at the python
boundary, avoiding per-trajectory I/O overhead at 10³+
parallelism. The bridge preserves exact bit-equivalence with
the Phase 2 emitter so the W₂ equivalence test
[[uq-compiled-vs-reference-w2-5sigma]] can compare paired
zarr stores directly.

investigations.name: pdmp-05-causal-discovery
investigations.description:
Phase 5 of the v2ecoli → PDMP roadmap. This is the payoff phase
— the one that closes the loop on the DUF ARC original goal of
simulation-based causal discovery in WCMs. It depends on every
preceding phase: the PDMP for process likelihoods (Phase 2), the
observation-likelihood library and accumulator (Phase 3), and the
compiled high-throughput runtime to make marginal-likelihood
estimation feasible (Phase 4).

The Bayesian-model-comparison framing puts each candidate gene-
function annotation in competition: each defines a different
WCM, marginalize over parameters, and compare via marginal
likelihoods. Russian Roulette estimators (Lyne et al. 2015)
provide unbiased estimates of these otherwise intractable
marginals.

Active causal inference (Toth et al. 2022) closes the experiment-
design loop: rather than passively observing, the agent proposes
interventions whose outcomes will most sharply distinguish
competing annotations. This converts annotation from
pattern-matching to hypothesis-driven discovery, in the spirit of
the DUF ARC vision.

The benchmark gene set should contain ≥20 E. coli genes with
literature-established functions across diverse mechanism
classes (kinases, transcription factors, transporters, structural
proteins, etc.) so that the validation isn't restricted to a
single functional category.

# Numerical considerations
Marginal likelihood numerics. Russian Roulette (Lyne et al. 2015)
produces unbiased estimators of intractable normalizing
constants Z = ∫ p(D|θ) p(θ) dθ via a truncated geometric series
with importance weights. The estimator can have unbounded
variance — we monitor the empirical variance over batches and
require an ESS-equivalent number of likelihood evaluations
N_eff ≥ 100 per Z estimate. If N_eff < 100 the result is flagged
and either (a) a tighter proposal is used, or (b) we fall back
to thermodynamic integration / nested sampling with documented
bias.

Bayes factor confidence intervals. We report log Bayes factors
with a 95% bootstrap CI from the RR variance bound, not point
estimates. Conclusions ("annotation A vs B is supported") only
fire if the CI sits entirely above the Jeffreys-scale threshold
(|log BF| > 1, "substantial evidence").

SBC at the model-comparison level. We extend SBC to model
comparison itself: for K=500 synthetic datasets each generated
under a known true annotation, the recovered posterior model
probability should be uniform conditional on the true model
index (Talts et al. 2018, Cook et al. 2006). A non-uniform
rank histogram signals systematic miscalibration of the
comparison pipeline before we trust it on novel annotations.

Active inference numerics. Expected information gain (EIG) is
estimated via nested Monte Carlo (outer over experiments, inner
over (θ, y) pairs). Standard NMC has bias O(1/N_inner) — we use
Donsker-Varadhan or DAD-MINE style variational lower bounds
where computationally feasible, falling back to NMC with explicit
bias bounds otherwise. Every intervention proposal carries its
EIG estimate ± MCSE; the loop never selects an intervention
whose EIG CI overlaps zero.

False discovery control. On benchmark recoveries, we report
per-annotation posterior probability AND a Benjamini-Hochberg
FDR at the gene-set level — q-value ≤ 0.1 required before
declaring a benchmark recovery successful.

Convergence rate of credible-interval widths. The claim that
credible interval widths shrink with sample size is only useful
if the rate is reported. Sub-√n is the standard MCMC rate
(variance of posterior mean ∝ 1/n_eff_samples); slower than
n^{-1/2} indicates a problem (poor mixing, non-identifiability)
and triggers diagnosis.

# Emitter
Each candidate-annotation run writes a zarr store containing
(a) the marginal-likelihood RR estimator trajectory, (b) per-
annotation posterior, (c) intervention-selection record + EIG
estimates. The benchmark gene-set sweep aggregates per-gene
zarr stores into a single zarr group per benchmark — readable
via xarray.open_mfdataset() for the BH-FDR summary at the
gene-set level.
